metaDescription: Compressor dehumidifiers under $200 for basements and big rooms, from 34 to 80 pint class, plus one quiet bedroom unit. Drain hose and rating tips inside.
expertTake: The KNKA 80 pint Energy Star unit is the top pick for a full basement because it pairs the biggest rating here with a long drain hose. The GoGuess 34 pint is the value pick for one damp room. Anyone who only needs a quiet bedroom unit should skip the compressors and take the BEDRED instead.
introParagraphs: At this level the choice stops being about tank size and starts being about water removal. Real compressor machines appear, with capacities rated in pints per day, and the question becomes how large a space you need to dry and where the water will go.

A machine that is too small runs constantly and still loses to the weather. A machine that is too large costs more than the room demands. The $200 cap reflects listing prices on the date this guide was updated, and prices move, so check before buying.

products.name: KNKA Energy Star 80 pint dehumidifier, 5500 sq ft, hose
products.description:
This KNKA is a compressor machine in the 80 pint class, with an Energy Star label that matters because it implies a meaningful efficiency threshold, not just a sticker. The listing gives two numbers, 80 pints per day at 95F and 95 percent humidity and 56 pints per day in typical basement conditions. The second figure is the one to plan around, and it still outworks every plate unit by a wide margin.

The built-in tank holds 1.45 gallons, and a 6.56 ft hose lets you drain continuously to a floor drain or sink. That is more than twice the length of the hose on the smaller KNKA 34 pint, which matters when the drain is across the room. The extra capacity does cost size and weight, and this is the loudest and bulkiest unit in this guide.

Expect a compressor-grade ownership routine. Wash the filter every few weeks, vacuum the coil once a year, and leave a foot of space behind it. If the hose sags, water backs up and the unit stops, so run it straight and downhill. For a finished or unfinished basement it is the machine in this tier that behaves like a real dehumidifier. Think about where the water goes before you buy.
products.bestFor: Full basements and large damp rooms with a floor drain.
pros: 80 pint class compressor with Energy Star label
Realistic 56 pint basement rating on the listing
Rated for up to 5500 sq ft
cons: Largest and loudest unit in this guide
Compressor life depends on filter care

products.name: DGVAM Energy Star dehumidifier, 45 to 80 pints, 4500 sq ft
products.description:
DGVAM markets a 45 to 80 pint adjustable output range, which suggests variable speed operation. In practice that means the machine can idle down once a room settles and ramp up when the humidity climbs. Built-in sensors track the room and adjust, aiming to hold a steady level instead of cycling hard on and off. That is easier on a compressor over several years.

Against the KNKA 80 pint, it covers 4500 square feet instead of 5500, which is a smaller rating but a more believable one for a single basement. It also includes a drain hose and automatic shutoff. The adjustable range makes it a good fit if you have a mixed space, such as a finished basement with an unfinished utility side.

Long-term care is the same: clean the filter, keep the coil free of dust and run the hose downhill. The adjustable range means it may run quieter at low output, though the listing does not give a decibel figure, so judge by how you use it. In the first month, watch the humidity reading and let the unit show you its working range. If it settles near 50 percent and cycles off, it is sized right; if it runs nonstop at 65 percent, the room needs the 80 pint KNKA instead.
products.bestFor: Mixed-use basements that need a variable output.
pros: Smart sensors hold a target humidity
Drain hose option for continuous running
cons: 4500 sq ft rating is below the KNKA 80
No decibel figure on the listing

products.name: GoGuess 34 pint compressor dehumidifier, 2500 sq ft
products.description:
The GoGuess is a compact compressor dehumidifier with three modes: Dehu, Turbo and Sleep. It includes auto humidity regulation, so it holds the room at a setpoint and stops when it gets there. Its max 34 pint rating is a peak figure at warm, humid test conditions, so plan for less in a cool basement.

It sits well below the KNKA 80 pint in capacity and rating, and it is smaller and lighter. That makes it the right size for a single damp bedroom, a laundry room or a small finished basement room. A drain hose connection removes the daily emptying chore.

Ownership is standard: clean the filter, vacuum the coil yearly and let it sit upright for a few hours after moving it. The Turbo mode runs the fan and compressor hard, which is loud, so use Sleep overnight. A sensible habit is to run Turbo for the first day on a wet room, then switch to Dehu and Sleep once the level drops. Constant Turbo wears the compressor faster and costs more power for no extra benefit at steady state.
products.bestFor: One damp room, laundry area or small finished basement.
pros: Real compressor at a moderate size
cons: 34 pint figure is a peak rating
Too small for a full basement

products.name: KNKA 34 pint dehumidifier, 2500 sq ft, 0.79 gal tank
products.description:
This KNKA is the small sibling of the 80 pint model, with a 0.79 gallon tank and a 3.28 ft included hose. Its Auto mode defaults to 50 percent humidity, a sensible target, and it has a Dry mode for faster laundry drying. It is a good fit for a single damp room.

Compared with the GoGuess it has nearly the same output and rating, so the decision comes down to controls and tank. The hose is shorter than the 80 pint KNKA's, so the drain must be close.

Care is the usual filter wash and yearly coil vacuum. Let it rest upright after transport, and keep it off carpet. It is a good fit beside a washer and dryer, where a shorter hose is plenty. Move it with the tank empty and let it stand upright a few hours afterward so the oil settles back in the compressor. Noise is the thing owners mention most with compressor boxes, so plan for a steady low hum with an occasional louder click as the compressor starts. A rubber mat under the feet reduces floor vibration.
products.bestFor: Laundry rooms and single damp rooms with a nearby drain.
cons: 34 pint figure is a peak rating

products.name: BEDRED 95 oz semiconductor dehumidifier, 1000 sq ft
products.description:
The BEDRED is a thermoelectric unit, not a compressor. Its 95 oz tank, sleep mode and auto shutoff make it suitable for a bedroom or bathroom. It is quiet and light, with a 7 colour ambient light.

Against the GoGuess it removes far less water, but it is silent where the compressor hums. Its 1000 sq ft rating is a ceiling for mild dampness.

It suits a bedroom with mild humidity. For a damp basement, the compressors above are the right tool. As a second machine it works well: run it in the bedroom while a compressor handles the basement below. That split keeps the sleeping area quiet and the wet area controlled, which a single mid-size unit cannot do. It also works as a nightstand-side partner to a basement compressor, handling the bedroom while the bigger machine handles the wet area.

buyingCriteria.explanation: The KNKA 80 pint unit quotes 80 pints at 95F and 95 percent humidity and 56 pints in basement conditions. The second is the planning number. Judge any unit by the lower figure and by the test condition printed beside it. For example, a 900 sq ft finished basement will keep the 34 pint GoGuess busy, whereas the DGVAM at 4500 sq ft will idle down.

A 34 pint unit like the GoGuess suits a single room. A 4500 to 5500 sq ft rating like the DGVAM or KNKA 80 suits a full basement. Buying too small means it runs constantly and never catches up. A common mistake is buying on the biggest number, then finding the unit too loud to leave on, so check where it will sit before you commit.

A hose works only if the drain is lower than the unit. The KNKA 80 includes a 6.56 ft hose, while the KNKA 34 has 3.28 ft. Measure the distance before choosing. If your drain is across the room, the 6.56 ft KNKA 80 hose reaches where the 3.28 ft hose will not.

A dehumidifier can run for months. The KNKA 80 and DGVAM carry Energy Star labels, which indicate better efficiency per pint. Over a damp season that saves real electricity. In a house with a nursery, a compressor in the basement and a plate unit upstairs is a sensible pairing.

Compressors hum and the Turbo mode on the GoGuess is loud. Put the machine in a utility area, not a bedroom, and use sleep mode at night. Plate units like the BEDRED stay silent but do little. Larger units draw several hundred watts, so read the label if you plan to run one all summer. Another point is that plate units like the BEDRED draw far less power than compressors, which counts if the room only needs gentle help.

Compressor coils frost below about 65 degrees F, so look for auto defrost. Output drops in cold air, so size up if your basement is cool. If your basement sits near 60 degrees, favour a model with defrost handling and expect lower output than the box says. Lastly, remember that every unit loses output as the air cools.

howWeEvaluated.title: Capacity and claim honesty
howWeEvaluated.description: We compared pint ratings and whether a realistic basement figure was given. The KNKA 80 was the only one to print both a peak and a basement number.

howWeEvaluated.title: Drainage options
howWeEvaluated.description: We scored hose length, tank size and the ease of continuous drainage. We favoured machines that print a realistic basement number as well as a peak number.

howWeEvaluated.title: Efficiency
howWeEvaluated.description: We looked for Energy Star labels and humidity sensors that avoid wasteful cycling.

howWeEvaluated.description: We weighed compressor hum against plate silence and the footprint of the 80 pint models.

cards.label: 80 pint class
cards.text: The KNKA 80 and DGVAM dry whole basements and carry Energy Star labels, but they are bulky and loud.

cards.label: 34 pint class
cards.text: The GoGuess and KNKA 34 suit single rooms and weigh less.

howToChoose.note: Choose 80 pint for a full basement; choose 34 pint for one room.

cards.label: Look for
cards.text: An 80 pint class rating, a long hose and Energy Star.

cards.label: In this comparison
cards.text: The KNKA 80 and DGVAM fit; the smaller units suit one room.

cards.label: Spend more if
cards.text: Your basement is over 5000 sq ft or often cold. A larger commercial type will outwork these.

cards.label: Save if
cards.text: You only need a bedroom fix. The BEDRED is enough.

maintenance.why: Dust blocks the coil. Output drops and the compressor works harder.
A kink or sag stops the machine.

faq.q: Which size should I buy for a basement?
faq.a: For a full basement choose the 80 pint class, the KNKA 80 or DGVAM. A 34 pint unit will run constantly. A rule of thumb is to size up one class when the basement has visible dampness or a musty smell.
Yes for a unit that runs for months. It lowers electric cost per pint. Energy Star is not a quality guarantee, but it does imply an efficiency threshold the cheapest units do not meet.
Often several years with clean filters. Dirty coils shorten life. Run the filter wash on a schedule and you remove the biggest cause of early failures.
It is a peak figure at 95F and 95% humidity. The KNKA 80 lists 56 pints for basement conditions. Always compare the test condition printed beside any pint figure.

Only if the drain is higher than the unit. These rely on gravity. If the drain is higher than the unit, you need a model with a built-in pump, which is not in this group. Check clearances on all sides, because blocked vents are the second most common cause of poor output.

faq.q: Can I use one in a bedroom?
faq.a: A compressor hums. Use the BEDRED for quiet. Use sleep mode and a hard flat surface for a quieter night.
